about: Every compile error and warning the spec names, with the pass that reports it, its codes and the target checks that prove it. cargo test -p mkp-cli --test rules fails when a rule has no check, a check doesn't expect its rule's code, or a code the compiler can report belongs to no rule.

rules.says: The grammar the other pages follow: source that no rule of it reads (an unclosed `{`, a missing expression, a character that is no token, a number running into a name) is not MKP.
A keyword can never be a name, after a dot included.
`$` on its own and `$abc` are neither keywords nor names, and in code each is a compile error whose message names `$state` (maths in code is a `latex` text literal, page 9).
MKP has no attributes: `#` is not a token in code, and in prose a `#` at the start of a line is always a Markdown heading.
Names are small, with `_` between words (`text_size`, `remove_where`); capitals only for a case after a dot or a type parameter on its own.
Type parameters are always capitals, so a reader sees at once which types in a signature are generic.
Every `let` and `mut`, field, input and parameter writes its type (`if (let c: text = …)` included, page 2).
Passed to an input, a parameter or an event, or given to a `let` that writes its type, a lambda may leave out its types; anywhere else it writes them all.
Every statement ends with a semicolon; a statement that is itself a block needs none.
An opening brace ends its line and a closing brace starts its own line; in code a compiler reports another layout as a warning and never reads it differently.
`==`, `!=`, the four comparisons and `in` don't chain: `a < b < c` is a compile error.
When `=` follows, the expression is the place assigned: a name, `self` or `$state`, with fields and items after it.
case = CAPS [ "(" name ":" type { "," name ":" type } ")" ]: a case's values have a name and a type, with no `mut` and no default.
token = "token" name ":" type [ implements ] "{" case { "," case } "}": a token type writes its value type after a colon, then cases.
pack = "pack" name "@" number "{" { packline ";" } "}", where a pack line is `uses`, `provides` or `implements`.
doc = "//@about" words | "//@param" name words | "//@deprecated" words, above a declaration.
A `//@param` that names no input is a compile error.
`//@deprecated use stats2, which shows a trend` makes every use of the declaration a warning with that text (page 6's Warnings table).
Only an `extern fn` may have a body, which is its default (an extern widget's block holds only slots, events and a markdown block, page 9).
file = "package" name ";" { import } { decl }: a pack's file starts with one package line.
A document has no `package` line and no `pack` block.
A document imports above its `@@@` line and writes no versions: `import kit;`.
A view statement outside a widget is a compile error: a .mkp file and a document's definitions never draw.
A `mut` at the top of a file is a compile error that points to `$state`, and a pack has no state of its own.
One `$state` block is something only a document has; in a .mkp file it is a compile error.
A pack's widget can't see `$state`: it takes what it shares as a `mut` input (page 9: a pack's files never read `$state`).
`$state`: one block, anywhere above the line, and a second one is a compile error.
`$state` is a value and never a type, so `$state {` starts no record: several fields change at once with `$state = $state with { … };`.
`$state`'s fields are written like a record's, each with its type and a starting value.
A document's shared variables are the fields of its `$state` block, which are variables without saying `mut`.
`expose` is written only at the top of a document, never in a pack or a widget.
An expose block's fns return nothing, take constant parameters, and may assign `$state`.
An expose block's fns are called only by the app, never by MKP code.
The first line that holds only `@@@` ends the definitions; a second unescaped `@@@` line is a compile error.
frontmatter = a line "---", YAML lines, a line "---", at the very top.
A line that starts with `@` and a small letter is always MKP: if it is not a call, a control line or a named slot, it is a compile error that says to write `\@`.
A call in prose is `@name`, its arguments in parentheses, then ` {` when a block follows or `;` when none does.
An opening brace ends its line and a closing brace starts its own line; in prose this is grammar, because it is how a block's end is found.
A block ends at the next line that holds only `}`, counting the blocks opened in between; a fenced code block inside it is skipped whole.
A line that holds only `}` ends a block; to show a line that holds only a brace, write `\}`.
A control line is `@if`, `@for`, `@mut for` or `@match`, with `} else {`, `} else if (…) {` and `case … {` lines inside.
"@match (" expr ") {" { "case" patterns " {" prose "}" } "}": a `@match` holds only `case … {` lines.
A named slot, `@slot name {`, is written only directly inside a call's block, for a widget with several slots.
A call, a control line or a closing `}` can't start inside a Markdown quote or list item: it is a compile error that says to use `@quote`, or `@bullets` and `@item`.
A line that holds only `$$` opens a maths block, and the next such line closes it.
In a sentence, `$` starts maths, so a bare `$state.tries` is shown as text, with a warning that says to put it in a hole.
A text literal is written between double quotes on one line.
A text literal's escapes are `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\u{…}` with a Unicode number in hex, and the hole.
A hole, `\{…}`, sits anywhere in a line, except in a code span or a fenced or indented code block (a text literal is on one line too).
One hole, always replaced: backslash and braces around an expression, in text, prose and maths.
`\{expr}` puts a value in text: the value has to fit `shown`, be a view, or be an `opt` of one.
A `text` can't hold a view, so a view in a hole of a `text` literal is a compile error.
A paragraph takes a `rich_text`, not an `opt`, so in prose and in a `markdown` block a paragraph with an `opt` hole is a compile error that names the hole (page 3, page 4 for literals in code).
An `md` holds blocks, so it goes in no hole: `@blocks(value = note);` places them.
A hole that `from` would have to read is a compile error that names the hole and says to build the record instead (pages 1, 2, 5 and 6 say the same).
For a literal, the compiler calls `from` at compile time, and `opt.NONE` is a compile error on the literal's own line, with the message of the rule that failed.
The values are written only in a `tokens` block, so a colour or a spacing written out anywhere else is a compile error (a plain value only where the token fits `literal<T>`).
A value is written `type.NAME = value;`, with a value of the token's type, and only inside a `tokens` block.
Every named case a `token` declaration lists needs a value from the pack that declares it.
Every `tokens` line names a declared token type.
Two visible cases with one name on one type are a compile error.
Only an implementer's pack may give a new value to a case that `core` declares; in any other pack, giving a `core` case a value is a compile error.
Every name is declared or imported, and declared once; core is imported by every file without saying so.
Every name is declared once: a declaration can't reuse a name that is already visible in its set.
A `let`, `mut`, parameter, input, slot, loop variable or fn can't take a name that is visible in the value set where it is declared.
`page.width` and `date.from(entry)`: a small name after the dot is a field or a fn, and when the value has no such field or fn, the compiler's message names the type too.
Every `type.CAPITALS` is a declared enum case or token case, counting the cases that `tokens` blocks add.
Every `@name` is a visible value or fn, with arguments in order, or a declared widget.
A slot, a fn that returns a view and a value that holds a view can't take the name of a visible widget (page 9: no slot has a widget's name).
A clash between two imported names, or an import and a declaration in the file, is a compile error on the import (page 1: rename one with `as`).
Two visible fns with one name on one type are a compile error, so one of them is imported under another name (page 6: on the import).
`provides` lists every name other packs may import; anything not listed can only be used inside the pack.
Everything is constant unless it says `mut`, a plain parameter or input is read-only, and to assign `a.b`, both `a` and `b` have to be mut.

`mut` on a parameter, an input or `self`, and a name opened with `if (mut …)`, write through to the value it stands for, and the caller has to pass something mutable (page 3: passing a constant to a `mut` input is a compile error).
`mut for` needs a `mut` list.
A variable with a wider contract than the `mut` input's is a compile error until it is narrowed, item by item for lists.
A `mut` value has to have exactly the type that is wanted, with no widening to `any`; its contract may be narrower.
The same variable, or a variable and a part of it, can't be passed to a `mut` parameter and to another parameter of the same call.
Plain `for` makes no copy: it can't change the list it walks or its items, and a change to them in its body is a compile error.
Once a body or an event handler removes `x` from its list, `x` can't be used in the rest of that block: a compile error when the compiler can see it.
A lambda can't assign a `mut` local of the fn it is written in.
A fn with a return type can't take a `mut` parameter.

A fn that returns a value changes nothing: it can't assign a `$state` field, a widget's own variable, a `mut` input, or a `mut for` or `if (mut …)` variable, only its own locals (a lambda follows the same table).
A fn with a return type may call an action only on its own `mut` local (`out.add(x)`).
Only a fn with no return type can `invoke` an event or call an `extern` fn that has no return type (page 6: an extern action is called only from event handlers, never while drawing).
A view, a `markdown` block, a `require`, a contract and a starting value can only call a fn that has a return type.
A `return x;` in a fn with no return type is a compile error that says to add one.
Using an `opt<color>` where a `color` is wanted is an ordinary type error: an opt value has to be opened before use.
Making a record: a field with `= value` can be left out, and one without must be given.
A fn on a type with `self` is called on a value, `s.line()`; one without is called on the type, `stat.blank("Deploys")`.
Plain fns take arguments in order, without names (an enum case is given its values in order, page 2).
Widget calls name every argument: `key = value`.
The caller sets an event to a fn with the same parameters and no return type (page 1: never to a call).
Every argument is named, is a declared input or event, and is set once.
Inputs go in the parentheses, slots go in the block, and setting anything twice is an error.
Every input without a default is given.
`==` stays strict: both sides are the same type.
`+` and `-` need numeric, and `*`, `/` and unary `-` need scaled: an operator is shorthand for an interface's fn (page 1: there is no `+` on text).
`==` and `!=` need same, and `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `in` need ordered (`view`, widgets and fns fit none of the six, so a view can't be compared, page 3).
A pack can't add `for` and `xs[i]` on its own types: `for` walks a list, a slot that holds a list, or a range, and `xs[i]` reaches into a list.
For an enum or a bool every case is listed, or `case else` takes the rest.
For a `number` or a `text`, `case else` is required, and so it is for a token: a pack may add cases to a token type.
`match` takes an enum, a `bool`, a `number` or a `text`.
Several cases can share one body, separated by commas, when none of them binds a name.
`for` walks a list or a range and `mut for` a `mut` list, so there is no while loop and a document can never hang a page.
walk = [ "mut" ] "for" "(" name [ "," name ] "in" expr ")" body: `mut` goes before `for`, and a loop has nothing after its list.
A constant where a contract is wanted is checked on the spot: out of range is a compile error on that line.
A value with no proof where a contract is wanted is a compile error that asks for one (assigning a mut value needs the same proof every time; a value under `try` needs none).
`add`, `insert`, `remove`, `remove_at` and `remove_where` are for lists with no length contract.
Bounds are always constants: a type can't depend on a value that is only known when the page runs.
A bound is a number with an optional sign, a duration, a named constant, or a constant expression in brackets.
A minus in a bound is a number's sign, so a negative name is written in brackets, `(-x)`.
A range after `text` is a compile error, because text has a length and `only` instead.
A range `low..high` is for numbers, durations, dates and a pack's own ordered types.
A whole range can't be negated: `-(1..10)` and `-x..5` are compile errors that point to `range.negate`.
In an expression a range's bounds are a number, a name or a bracketed expression, so `0..n - 1` is a type error.
Two contracts that can't both hold, such as `int step 0.5`, are a compile error.
`only (…)` lists the allowed values, for types that implement `same`, and the values are constants.
A record's `require` blocks run when it is made: at compile time for constants, where a `false` is a compile error.
In a widget, a `require` reads inputs only; with constant inputs it is checked by the compiler.
A division by zero, and a result too large for decimal128, are failures, or compile errors when the compiler can see them.
The compiler uses the same limits (items, steps, depth) when it runs `from`, `require` and contracts on constants, where passing one is a compile error.
A record or an enum may hold its own type only inside a `list` or an `opt`.
`implements` is a checked promise, written where the type is declared: a missing field or fn is reported on that line.
An interface can't ask for a `mut` field.
Type arguments are never written at a use, so every type parameter has to appear in a parameter, an input, a field or a slot.
A bound `T: labelled` names an interface, with its type arguments if it has any.
A bare interface name is never a type on its own: `chart` alone as a type is a compile error that points to both `any chart` and `<T: chart>`.
`any` works for an interface that uses `self` only in front of the dot or as a return type; `any same`, `any ordered` and `any numeric` are compile errors.
A widget body is, in this order: `param` inputs, `slot`s, `event`s, `require` blocks, its own `mut` and `let` variables, its fns, `view`, and `markdown` last.
Only `view` and `markdown` are required in a widget body.
A widget declared in a document may leave out `markdown`; in a .mkp file the block is required.
An empty block, `markdown { }`, says the widget writes nothing; the compiler warns where such a widget is declared.
A document widget's built Markdown uses the starting values, so a branch that depends on a variable, a `$state` field or the widget's own, gets a warning naming the line.
A block of children, a slot's block and a `view` block all hold the same five things and nothing else: `let`, `if`, `for`, `match`, and views.
There is no assignment in a view, so `name = value;` in a block is always an input.
A block is read by its first word, children or the named form, and the two can't be mixed.
A block of children goes to a widget with exactly one slot; a widget with several slots gets one named block per slot.
A named block, or a `@slot` line in prose, names a real slot.
A slot is declared in the widget's body with `slot`, and filled only by a block, never with `=`.
A slot with a widget type takes only calls of that type, with `for`, `if` and `match` around them; text, other widgets and helpers that return `view` are compile errors there.
A length contract on a slot is checked by the compiler when the children are written out one by one.
A call that returns a view is always written with `@`: `tile(s)` without it is a compile error.
Only a `view`, a widget type, `any` of a widget interface, or a type parameter bounded by a widget interface can be placed with `@` (page 3: other values are skipped after `@`).
A view value can be held in a `let`, returned, passed to an input and placed; it can't be held in a `mut` variable.
The inputs of a widget value can be read, `t.title`, but they can't be assigned.
The inputs of a widget value can be read; its events can't be reached.
A chain of `sizing` around one child is folded into one set of properties, and setting one property twice in a chain is a compile error.
A spot outside the bounds is a warning: at compile time when both are constants.
Raw HTML is shown as text, so an HTML comment in prose shows: the compiler warns and points to `@//`, prose's comment.
An MKP fn fits a shader's type too, but the runtime calls it for each pixel within the step limit, so only small areas fit, and the compiler warns.
A fn type, `fn(item: T): bool`: a value of it is called with its arguments, and nothing else can be called.
A migration belongs to the pack of the version it moves to, and holds a block per changed declaration, headed by its kind and its old name, and fns of its own.
A surface holds declarations only: each widget and fn as an extern signature, and records, enums, token types, tokens blocks, aliases, interfaces and let constants as they were.
A pack is compared with the surface of its own version: a change that could break a use is a compile error that says to make a new version.
No fixtures for now: the core library's tests belong in the target checks, so `fixture` and `assert` are not part of MKP.
